SOAX is the better value for residential and mobile work: US traffic costs $5/GB on Sandbox and $3/GB on its $200 Builder plan against Bright Data's $8 list price, mobile and residential share one rate, and Tier 3 countries are much cheaper. Bright Data is the better choice when you need datacenter or ISP proxies (SOAX discontinued both), managed unblocking, a SERP API or the Scraping Browser, and carrier-level precision at enterprise scale. Remember that SOAX credits expire after 60 days.

Bright Data and SOAX both run large residential and mobile networks with fine-grained targeting, and both are popular with ad-verification teams. Bright Data adds datacenter and ISP proxies, managed unblocking and SERP products, and mature compliance processes, at the top of the price range. blocks.text: Bright Data in 2026: what you get

Bright Data, formerly Luminati, is the default enterprise pick for teams that want every collection tool under one contract. Its residential pool is one of the deepest available (150M+ advertised IPs across 195 countries), targeting goes down to city, ZIP and ASN, and the company layers managed products such as Web Unlocker and the Scraping Browser on top. You pay for that breadth: entry pricing is the highest of the major providers unless a promotion is running, and access to some target categories requires a compliance review.

Strengths: Deepest targeting in the market (ZIP, ASN, carrier); Managed unblocking, SERP and browser products under one account; Mature compliance and KYC processes that enterprise buyers ask for; Very large residential pool for high-rotation work. Weak spots: Highest list price per GB at low volume; Dashboard and zone setup take time to learn; Some targets need a compliance review before access.
SOAX in 2026: what you get

SOAX is a residential and mobile specialist known for granular filtering. Its 2026 pricing replaced fixed GB bundles with plans (Sandbox, Builder, Team, Scale, Enterprise) that include credits, and the credit burn rate depends on the exit country's tier. That makes SOAX cheap for some geographies and expensive for low-volume US work. The network is large (155M residential, 33M mobile advertised) and supports protocols few competitors offer, including UDP and QUIC.

Strengths: Residential and mobile on one balance; UDP and QUIC support alongside SOCKS5; Large pool with city and ISP targeting on every plan; Cheap traffic for Tier 2 and Tier 3 countries. Weak spots: Credits expire after 60 days; US traffic is expensive on small plans; Datacenter and ISP proxies were discontinued.
Pricing: Bright Data vs SOAX

Bright Data lists residential traffic at $8/GB pay-as-you-go with no commitment, and it frequently runs 50%-off promotions that bring that to about $4/GB. Monthly plans start with the Growth tier at $499 for roughly 141 GB (about $3.50/GB) and fall to around $2.50/GB on the largest public plan.

SOAX bills prepaid credits. For US (Tier 1) traffic, the no-fee Sandbox plan costs $5/GB, Builder ($200/month) $3/GB, Team ($500/month) $2.20/GB, and Scale ($1,500/month) $1.50/GB; cheaper countries cost less (Tier 3 from $2/GB on Sandbox). Credits expire 60 days after purchase, and SOAX counts traffic in both directions.

For a 10 GB month, SOAX costs about $50 while Bright Data costs about $80, so SOAX saves around 38%. For a 100 GB month, SOAX costs about $300 while Bright Data costs about $499, so SOAX saves around 40%. Both Bright Data and SOAX work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

On paper the two networks are similar in size: Bright Data advertises 150M+ residential IPs and SOAX advertises 155M residential + 33M mobile. Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, Bright Data lists 195 countries and SOAX lists 195. On targeting, Bright Data offers country, state, city, ZIP, ASN and carrier, while SOAX offers country, region, city and ISP; ASN and ZIP on Scale plans.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, Bright Data offers rotating per request or sticky sessions you control per zone, and SOAX offers rotating or sticky; mobile sessions up to 60 minutes. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: its pool depth and Web Unlocker handle hardened targets. How SOAX compares: a large pool and its own error headers help debugging.

SERP and rank tracking: Bright Data wins. The deciding factor for Bright Data: it sells a dedicated SERP API alongside raw proxies. The limitation on the SOAX side: city and ISP targeting for local results.

Social media and multi-account management: SOAX wins. The deciding factor for SOAX: mobile IPs on the same balance as residential. The limitation on the Bright Data side: it is powerful but expensive for low-volume account work.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: ZIP-level targeting suits local pricing and stock checks. How SOAX compares: granular location filters.

Ad verification and geo-testing: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Bright Data: carrier and ASN targeting reproduce what real users see. With SOAX: ISP, ASN and carrier-level targeting. Run the same small test on both before committing.
Tight budgets: SOAX. SOAX has the edge here. Why: cheap in Tier 3 countries but pricey for small US jobs. How Bright Data compares: its list price is the highest in this comparison.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Bright Data: Free trial for business accounts, no card required. SOAX: Paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99. Verification and payment rules differ too. Bright Data: Verification required for some sensitive targets. SOAX: Verification for postpaid and enterprise terms. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Bright Data and SOAX before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle Bright Data vs SOAX faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Bright Data: free trial for business accounts, no card required; SOAX: paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99).

2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day. 3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Bright Data comes out ahead in 3, SOAX in 2, and 1 is a tie. That makes Bright Data the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Bright Data is strongest for enterprise data teams with budget for managed tooling, while SOAX is strongest for mobile-first work such as app testing and social platforms. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
